title: Rumi's tomb
hook: in Konya, his tomb is visited by people of many backgrounds
tomorrow: a survivor's prayers. why would anyone call them psalms?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hare, a lion, and a well, where the lion leaped at his own face. Wit over weight. Today, the last stop in Rumi's book: his own resting place.

Flowers left at a gate. Candles outside a venue after a singer dies. Notes taped to a wall by people who never met the person. Saying goodbye to someone you only knew through their words is its own kind of grief. For Rumi, there's a place to go. In Konya, in Turkey, his tomb stands under a tiled dome, and people come: Muslims, and visitors of many backgrounds, some who've read every line and some who know one. So where would you go to say goodbye to Rumi? There.
screen: `FLOWERS AT A GATE.` → `A TOMB IN KONYA.` → `PEOPLE OF MANY BACKGROUNDS.`

segments.voice: Aflaki, who wrote down stories of Rumi's circle, tells of his funeral: tradition says Christians and Jews walked with the Muslims behind the bier, weeping, each saying in their own way that he had taught them something. Whatever the details, the scene has stuck to the place. The welcome is still part of it. A verse is hung near the tomb and printed on cards: come, come again, whoever you are, even if you've broken your promise again and again, come. Here's the honest part. Some scholars of Persian poetry say the verse isn't found in Rumi's own works, and trace it to an earlier poet. It may not be his. But it has become his door, and it says something the Qur'an says first: don't despair of God's mercy, because He forgives. Coming back is always allowed. That's what the tomb gives a person this week. Maybe you've drifted. Maybe it's been a long time since you prayed, or went to the masjid, or opened the book. Maybe you feel like a fraud walking back in. The door at Konya, and the verse on it, say the same thing a door of mercy says: you're not too late, and you're not the first. Come, come again.
screen: `AFLAKI: MOURNERS OF OTHER FAITHS.` · `A VERSE ON THE DOOR.` · `MAYBE NOT HIS. STILL HIS DOOR.` · `DON'T DESPAIR OF MERCY.` · then, large: `COME, COME AGAIN.`

segments.voice: If you pray, ask mercy for Rumi in whatever words come; Muslims say rahimahullah, may God have mercy on him, after the name of someone who has died. Or say aloud the name of one teacher, living or gone, whose words still reach you, and thank them out loud.
screen: `MERCY FOR RUMI.` · `OR: NAME ONE TEACHER, ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Rumi's tomb: his resting place in Konya, where people of many backgrounds come, and a verse at the door says come again.
For anyone who's been away a while: come, come again, however long it's been. All eight of Rumi's stories, told.

screen: `DAY 1636 COUNTS.` → `RUMI'S MASNAVI · 8 OF 8.` → `TOMORROW: A SURVIVOR'S PRAYERS. WHY CALL THEM PSALMS?`

howItsDone: Visitors to Rumi's tomb in Konya, now a museum, file past his sarcophagus; Muslims among them recite al-Fatiha or ask mercy for him, and others stand in silence.

notes: Aflaki's account of the funeral is hagiography; the voice frames it as 'tradition says'. Confirm.

The 'come, come again' quatrain: often credited to Rumi, but some scholars attribute it to Abu Sa'id Abi'l-Khayr or find it absent from Rumi's Divan/Masnavi; the voice says 'some scholars… may not be his'. Paraphrased (not a quotation of any modern translation). Confirm.
'Muslims say rahimahullah' in the practice: a common formula; a Keeper may prefer 'Muslims say'.
'Tiled dome': the tomb's dome is tiled (the 'Green Dome'); color omitted. howItsDone says the tomb is now a museum (the Mevlana Museum); confirm.
